The work described in Task 8.1 demonstrated the communication and control techniques required to integrate various DERs into the grid in order to provide grid services. Despite the large and varied DERs under control as a part of this project, the total aggregation of all DERs was still a small fraction of the total load 21 on the Western Interconnection, which means that the response of these resources would have a minimal impact on the frequency of the system. One goal of the hardware-in-the-loop development is to model the impact of this project’s DER control strategies at a larger scale, where the resources under control represent a much larger fraction of the total interconnection’s load and generation. This scaling-up of the project’s DERs was accomplished by taking the response of the DER devices in hardware and applying them to a model of the grid in simulation that was much smaller than the real power system. This includes a model of a local distribution network feeding the DERs and a model of a generation fleet whose frequency changed as a result of imbalances between generation and load. The distribution network is modeled in the Open Distribution Simulation System (OpenDSS). The network contains a substation which feeds various distribution lines, uncontrolled loads, and DER devices. The power of the uncontrolled loads is defined ahead of time, while the DER loads are updated in real-time using the data collected from the real DER devices participating in this project. One additional input to the model is a source of a disturbance in power, which can be a positive or negative value, representing unscheduled variations in total system load. Key outputs of the distribution model include power flows on the power delivery equipment and voltages at each node on the network. These outputs allow USU to estimate the quantity of grid services that can be provided while constrained by the capacity of the distribution network, and how these devices can be used to alleviate capacity challenges on the distribution network. Another key output of the distribution model is the total power consumption of the network. This includes both the controlled and uncontrolled loads but also the power losses in the distribution network that feeds the loads. The losses are important for measuring the performance of the grid services at the regional level, as a change in power output by a DER will result in a change in power equal to its measured power change plus the change in losses induced elsewhere on the distribution network. The total power change simulated in the distribution network is fed to a generator model, which models the frequency of the synchronous grid.
